title: Majh ki Var close
hook: a ballad that asks everyone to live up to their own name

segments.voice: Yesterday the ballad said it is hard to be called a true Muslim: first let the faith be sweet, then let pride go. Your line was hard to be true. Where did your own faith, or your own word, ask more of you than you expected? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

To take what belongs by right to someone else is pork to the Muslim and beef to the Hindu. That's a salok in Guru Nanak's ballad in Majh, given here in plain English, not word for word. It names a food each of his neighbors refuses, and it doesn't ask either one to give that refusal up. It borrows the full weight of it and points it somewhere new: at the coin, the hour, the credit that was never yours. Two names, one measure. Today the Var in Majh closes on this page, and on the question it leaves with everyone who hears it.
screen: `ANOTHER'S RIGHT.` → `PORK TO ONE, BEEF TO THE OTHER.` → `TWO NAMES, ONE MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Look back over the Var as this path has walked it. It opened with the Guru as giver, a cool house of ice, a lamp. It named an age like a knife, where kings turn butcher. Yesterday it said it is hard to be called a Muslim, and asked that mercy be the mosque. Today's salok, on the same page as yesterday's, widens the circle. It speaks to Muslim and Hindu in one breath, each in the terms of their own practice. Here is how it goes on, in paraphrase. The Guru and the pir will stand up for you only if you don't eat what is carrion. Talk alone doesn't carry anyone to paradise; release comes from practicing truth. Adding spice to forbidden food doesn't make it lawful. Notice three things. First, the measure is the same for both. Neither neighbor is ranked above the other; each is held to a line they already keep, and asked to keep it in a new place. Second, the new place is ordinary. Not a shrine, not a feast day. It's what you take: a share, a seat, a turn in line, the credit for someone else's work. Third, words don't settle it. Fine talk, the salok says, gets no one there. The ballad has been doing this from its first stanzas: holding a name, king, believer, Muslim, Hindu, up beside a life, and asking whether the two match. Some readers hear it asking the same of anyone who carries a name, Sikhs included. So the Var in Majh closes here for us. A name is honored when the life under it takes nothing that isn't its own. That's today's line.
screen: `GIVER, KNIFE, HARD TO BE TRUE.` · `ONE MEASURE FOR TWO NEIGHBORS.` · `NOT A SHRINE: WHAT YOU TAKE.` · `TALK DOESN'T CARRY YOU.` · then, large: `LIVE UP TO YOUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live up to your name. Let the breath slow first. Then walk through the day ahead in your mind, hour by hour: the work, the meals, the talk, the messages. Look for one place where something could slip into your hands that isn't quite yours. Someone else's turn, the credit for a shared idea, the last of something meant to be split. Don't judge it. Just mark it. Then see yourself, at that moment, leaving it where it belongs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath out. The bell holds the time.
Majh ki Var close. Guru Nanak's ballad in Raga Majh, a run of stanzas and saloks that holds each name, Muslim and Hindu alike, up against a life. Today's word.
Your line: live up to your name. When the moment you marked in the sit comes, leave what isn't yours where it belongs. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Majh ki Var in kirtan and katha at the gurdwara, and teachers may linger on its saloks that hold believers of every name to the same plain honesty.
